scenes.narration: Two hundred thousand miles from home, a bang shook the spacecraft. Warning lights came on. Oxygen was venting into space, and the three men aboard were losing the power, water and air they needed to survive.
This is the story of how they came home anyway, and of the cardboard, plastic and tape that helped keep them alive.

Apollo 13 launched on April 11, 1970, with Jim Lovell in command, Jack Swigert flying the command module and Fred Haise flying the lunar module. It was meant to be the third crewed landing on the Moon.
On April 13, an oxygen tank in the service module exploded. Swigert radioed the words that became famous: Houston, we've had a problem. The landing was over. Survival was the only mission left.
The crew moved into the lunar module, Aquarius, and used it as a lifeboat. It was built to support two men for two days. Now it had to keep three men alive for four.

Carbon dioxide began to build up. The command module's square filter canisters did not fit the lunar module's round openings, so engineers on the ground designed an adapter from plastic bags, cardboard and tape, and talked the crew through building it.
They swung around the Moon and headed home. On April 17, 1970, the command module splashed down in the South Pacific, and the crew was recovered by the USS Iwo Jima. All three men were alive.

youtube.title: The Cardboard Fix That Saved Apollo 13
youtube.description:
An explosion two days into the flight ended the Moon landing and started a four-day fight to get three astronauts home.

Source: NASA, Apollo 13 Mission Report (MSC-02680), 1970.
